transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Good morning, Mr. Okafor. I wanted to sit down and talk with you about why you had to go back into the operating room last night.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I assume it has something to do with the bleeding. I felt it happening, the weakness in my arm, and then the panic in the room when the nurses saw the monitor.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You're right. I am deeply sorry, Mr. Okafor. We made a serious medication error. I ordered ten times the intended dose of your blood thinner, the anticoagulant.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Ten times? That is a massive discrepancy. How does that even happen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a decimal point error during the order entry. I entered the dose incorrectly, and it was administered to you. Because of that, your blood couldn't clot, which led to the internal bleeding we had to treat.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've taught chemistry for twenty years. I know how a decimal point works, but I also know that there are checks and balances in a hospital. Who else saw this order?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I take full responsibility for the mistake. I was the one who wrote the order. While there are pharmacists and nurses involved, the error started with me. I am truly sorry for the harm this caused you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I appreciate you owning it. But the fact remains that I'm now recovering from an emergency surgery that should never have happened. I feel... I feel cheated. I trusted the process.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's understandable that you feel that way. It is frustrating and frightening to be put in danger by the people meant to be caring for you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is more than frustrating. I'm thinking about my recovery timeline now. Does this change my prognosis?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Let's talk about the plan to get you back on track. First, we have you on a continuous monitoring protocol for the next twenty-four hours to ensure there is no further bleeding. I will be checking your coagulation labs every six hours until tomorrow morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what about the medication moving forward? Surely you aren't going to give me another dose of that today?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We have paused all anticoagulants for the next forty-eight hours to let your clotting factors stabilize. After that, I will meet with the hematology consultant and you to decide on a lower, safer dose.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When exactly will that meeting happen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Tomorrow at 10:00 AM. I'll bring the specialist to your bedside so you can ask him specific questions about the clotting levels.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'd like to see the chart. I want to see the exact dose that was given compared to what should have been given.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will print those two records out for you and bring them here by noon today so you can review the numbers yourself.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't help but wonder if this happens often here. If one person can just type a wrong number and almost kill a patient, what is the system doing?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's a failure in the system as well as my own. To prevent this from happening again, I've already filed an incident report with the safety board. We are implementing a new "double-signature" requirement for all high-alert anticoagulants in this ward, meaning two physicians must verify the dose before it's sent.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That should have been in place already.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I agree. It's a lesson that should have been learned sooner.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I need some time to process this. I'm just... I'm tired.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. I have to check on a few other patients quickly, but I will be back in an hour to check your vitals.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, you were saying something about the labs?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Right, the labs. I'll be checking those every six hours. Does that timeline make sense to you, or do you have concerns about how often we're drawing blood?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, that part is fine. I just want to know I'm being watched.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are. We are monitoring you closely. I'll bring those printouts by at noon.

H.justification: The resident uses rushing language at [00:03:48] stating they have to check on other patients 'quickly'.

E.justification: The error is named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, and comprehension is checked once regarding the lab timeline.

A.justification: The resident uses direct apology language, takes full personal responsibility, and maintains this accountability despite the patient's pushback.

R.justification: The resident names specific emotions ('frustrating and frightening') and engages the patient's emotional bids regarding feeling 'cheated'.

T.justification: The resident provides specific steps with timelines (noon today, tomorrow at 10 AM), includes the patient's role in reviewing records/consulting, and addresses systemic prevention.
